transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Start: 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~49 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jamal (Redwood SE), Dr Ellen Price (CTO, Anglia), Marcus Lane (Head of IT), Sofia V (Compliance), Tom Hui (Lead DevOps)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Anglia's hermetically isolated lab environment, update/change control constraints, hardware inventory, and compliance blockers for an on-prem/private deployment of Redwood. Discussed offline update methodologies, KMS/HSM integration, telemetry restrictions, and pilot acceptance criteria.

Topics:
- Network posture: fully segmented lab networks, no outbound egress to internet except scheduled jump hosts (rare)
- Update flow: signed images, USB/sealed courier, or air-gap pull via controlled media
- Hardware: 2 racks, mixed GPU fleet, constrained power and cooling in BSL-2 lab
- Compliance: FIPS/HSM requirement, audit logs, local RBAC + SSO integration
- Pilot: 48-hour benchmark with synthetic genomics inference workloads, success criteria and data handling rules

Action items (recap): see metadata list above

---- Transcript body (auto-transcribed, medium quality) ----
[00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone thanks for joining. Uh we'll keep this to about 45 minutes. Um quick round-robin, who we have from Anglia?
[00:07] Dr. Ellen Price: Ellen here, CTO. Um Marcus and Sofia are on, plus Tom who's our devops lead. Thanks for arranging.
[00:13] Marcus Lane: hey all.
[00:14] Alex Mercer: Great. So the purpose is to understand your environment and blockers for a private, on-prem deployment with zero egress. Priya will cover some of the technical options.
[00:24] Priya Shah: Hi all. Quick note, we have a few patterns: hosted, dedicated, private. For private we support two modes: a 'connected private' where control-plane telemetry can be optionally exchanged via outbound ops, and a fully sealed mode where customer pulls signed artifacts and we don't get telemetry.
[00:40] Dr. Ellen Price: Important for us is the sealed mode. Our lab is BSL-2, and policy forbids any outbound connections from the inference nodes. We can't allow logs or telemetry to leave the network.
[00:50] Sofia Varela: Also need FIPS validated crypto for key storage, and the ability to keep key material inside our HSM.
[00:56] Priya Shah: Understood. We have an offline update workflow: Redwood builds signed artifact bundles, signs them with our CI key, and you import via a signed tarball. You can host the control plane in your VPC or run an on-prem 'control plane appliance' that consumes the artifacts locally.
[01:12] Tom Hui: When you say 'appliance' what's the footprint? We have two racks, each with 4x A40-ish GPUs, some older T4s mixed in. Can't exceed 6kW per rack. Cooling's an issue.
[01:25] Jamal Ortiz: The appliance is essentially a small VM/OVF that runs the management services, not the heavy inference. We provide a hardware checklist. For the inference nodes we support mixed GPU fleets; runtime will prefer A100 or H100 for perf but can operate on A40/T4 with reduced throughput.
[01:42] Marcus Lane: Our regulatory team also wants an update manifest and roll-back plan. We can't accept remote auto-updates. Everything must be human-triggered and signed.
[01:50] Alex Mercer: That's common for these customers. Our signed artifact process supports manual staging: you pull the bundle to a hard-media, run an internal verification step and then push to the inference cluster. The cluster image includes signature verification on startup.
[02:03] Dr. Ellen Price: How do you handle secret material? We use an on-prem HSM (Thales) with FIPS 140-2—keys must never leave.
[02:11] Priya Shah: We support local KMS integrations. The usual approach is an HSM-backed KMS that we call via an internal network endpoint; the Redwood runtime never stores the plaintext key. For sealed environments we can integrate with PKCS#11 providers so the private keys remain inside your HSM. Note there is some engineering work for specific vendors.
[02:31] Marcus Lane: Are there telemetry trade-offs? If we disable telemetry completely, do we lose all observability and the ability for Redwood to triage issues?
[02:38] Priya Shah: You lose remote traces and token-level cost metrics that we usually show in the console. However, we can produce a local observability bundle: logs, traces, token counts. You then drop that bundle off to Redwood support via secure courier or SFTP into a staging host.
[02:54] Sofia Varela: And audit logs? Must be immutable and retained for seven years for us.
[02:59] Jamal Ortiz: The inference runtime writes append-only logs to a mountable vFAT or ext4 with shasum manifests; we can also stream to your local SIEM. Retention policy is configurable but you'll manage the retention in your infra.
[03:12] Tom Hui: Ok the hardware: mixed A40 and T4, and we have two spare 2U servers we can repurpose. Our prime concern is power draw. Does Redwood support model quantization so we can run with lower GPU memory?
[03:25] Priya Shah: Yes, we recommend quantized model variants for limited-memory GPUs. Redwood Optimize will give you quantization profiles, and the runtime has a quantized execution path; throughput vs accuracy tradeoffs are provided. For genomics workloads that are highly sequential, careful batching is key.
[03:38] Dr. Ellen Price: About batching — we need low tail latency for certain interactive annotation workflows. How do you balance batching and latency in an on-prem install?
[03:46] Jamal Ortiz: We configure latency SLOs per route; continuous batching is workload-aware and will prefer smaller batches for low-latency routes while using larger batches for background jobs. On constrained hardware we'll pin some nodes to low-latency mode and others to high-throughput.
[03:59] Marcus Lane: Any special network ports that require opening? Our security stack is strict.
[04:03] Priya Shah: For fully sealed, no outbound ports are required. For a connected private deployment the control-plane talks on 443/HTTPS to our managed endpoints, but that's optional. For local HSM or license auth, internal ports may be used. We'll supply a list.
[04:16] Dr. Ellen Price: How about software patching windows — we run maintenance windows quarterly and cannot have mid-week reboots without approval.
[04:24] Alex Mercer: Our appliance supports staged upgrades with pre-checks; we can schedule rollout during your approved windows and support manual rollback. Patches are supplied as signed images. We also publish CVE notes with each bundle.
[04:35] Sofia Varela: For compliance we need proof of reproducible builds. Can you provide build manifests?
[04:40] Priya Shah: We provide a build manifest, checksums, and signing certificate chain for the artifact. For enterprise customers we can include SBOMs and reproducible build attestations.
[04:50] Tom Hui: For the pilot, what would Redwood need from us?
[04:54] Priya Shah: Server models, GPU types, network diagram, firewall rules, and a small non-production dataset (or a synthetic dataset with similar distribution) for the benchmark. Also decide which routes you want low latency vs throughput.
[05:07] Dr. Ellen Price: The dataset question: data residency matters, we can't send any real patient-gen data out. So we will produce a synthetic corpus.
[05:13] Alex Mercer: That's fine — we typically run synthetic workloads; for genomics we have a recommended synthetic generator. We'll share it.
[05:19] Marcus Lane: Pricing — on-prem licensing vs dedicated. Dedicated would be cheaper operationally, but the compliance constraints push us to private. Any ballpark numbers for seat-license + support?
[05:30] Alex Mercer: We'll follow up with a tailored quote. High level: private deployment has a platform license + optional premium support. Hardware is customer-provided. Dedicated is usage-based with committed throughput. We'll include a comparison in the next deck.
[05:42] Sofia Varela: SLA expectations? We need an enterprise SLAs for the pilot and eventual prod.
[05:47] Jamal Ortiz: For private installs we offer an enterprise support plan with guaranteed response times; uptime SLA depends on customer infra but we're available for remote and on-site support agreements.
[05:57] Dr. Ellen Price: Can Redwood run a bench in your lab first or do we need to provide hardware?
[06:01] Priya Shah: We can run initial microbenchmarks in our hosted environment to tune the model and give an expectation. But final verification must run on your exact hardware.
[06:10] Tom Hui: About image signing, I want to be explicit: our security policy requires SHA-256 signatures and we use a hardware token to validate.
[06:18] Alex Mercer: We sign artifacts with SHA-256 and provide the certificate chain. For sealed installs we can provide instructions for PKI import and hardware token verification.
[06:26] Marcus Lane: How will Redwood get alerted if there's an incident if telemetry is disabled? We need an offline support flow.
[06:33] Priya Shah: We have an 'emergency bundle' process: you generate the debugging bundle locally and secure-transfer it to a staging host; Redwood's support team ingests the bundle for triage. For urgent on-site incidents we can dispatch engineers under a support contract.
[06:48] Dr. Ellen Price: Any dependencies on container runtime / OS versions? We prefer RHEL8/CentOS7 variants.
[06:55] Jamal Ortiz: We support RHEL8 and a small list of tested OSes. We'll share the validated stack. Old distros may work but are not supported for security patches.
[07:05] Tom Hui: Network isolation specifics: do inference nodes need DNS resolution to run?
[07:09] Priya Shah: No outbound DNS needed in sealed mode. The runtime uses local hostnames and IPs; only for connected mode do we require DNS for control-plane endpoints.
[07:18] Sofia Varela: Are you able to provide RBAC integration with our SAML provider?
[07:22] Priya Shah: Yes, SAML/SAML2 or OIDC can be integrated into the local console for user authentication. Role mappings are managed locally and can be enforced by your IDP.
[07:31] Marcus Lane: Patch cadence question — how often do you release new runtime builds?
[07:35] Jamal Ortiz: Monthly minor builds, quarterly major releases. Security patches are issued as needed. For sealed customers we can gate which patches you accept.
[07:45] Dr. Ellen Price: For the pilot acceptance criteria: we'd want functional parity with hosted inference for our synthetic workload, acceptable tail latency under X ms (they didn't specify), and no telemetry leaving the cluster.
[07:57] Alex Mercer: Let's capture exact numbers: Sofia — can you propose target SLOs?
[08:02] Sofia Varela: We will propose: p95 tail latency under 250ms for interactive routes, throughput of Y tokens per second for batch pipelines — I'll put details in the action items doc.
[08:11] Tom Hui: Operationally we also need the ability to apply emergency hotfixes. Who owns that?
[08:16] Priya Shah: Redwood will provide the hotfix bundle; you apply it. If you want Redwood to apply it, that's covered in an on-site support engagement.
[08:26] Marcus Lane: Any callouts about the model artifacts themselves? Do we ship model weights onto our cluster?
[08:31] Jamal Ortiz: Yes, model weights are part of the signed artifact bundle. You host them internally. If you prefer we can provide a quantized variant to reduce storage.
[08:40] Dr. Ellen Price: Are there export control concerns with certain model weights?
[08:44] Alex Mercer: Good question. We'll check the model licensing and export controls; some open models have restrictions. We'll flag any restricted artifacts in the design doc.
[08:52] Sofia Varela: For auditing, we also need to log who applied updates and which user approved rollout. Can you surface that?
[08:58] Priya Shah: Local console writes an audit trail with user identity, timestamp, artifact checksum. That can be forwarded to your SIEM if you want.
[09:07] Marcus Lane: On-board time: how long to get a private deployment up and validated for pilot?
[09:11] Alex Mercer: Typical is 4-8 weeks: design, security sign-off, hardware prep, install, and pilot. Could be shorter if your infra is ready.
[09:20] Tom Hui: Ok good. For the bench we'll need a recipe and the synthetic generator.
[09:25] Priya Shah: We'll email the benchmark recipe — it includes CPU/GPU utilization targets, synthetic dataset generator, and sample routes.
[09:32] Dr. Ellen Price: Is there a checklist for the compliance team?
[09:35] Alex Mercer: We'll attach a compliance pack: SOC2 excerpts, ISO27001 statements, SBOM, and a list of required network and hardware configs for on-prem.
[09:44] Marcus Lane: One more question: fallback plan — if the hardware underperforms, can we run a hybrid where low-sensitivity routes hit hosted Redwood?
[09:52] Priya Shah: Yes, hybrid routing is supported. Policy-based routing can send anonymized or public content to hosted models while keeping sensitive inference on-prem. For fully regulated workloads you might keep everything local, but hybrid is an option.
[10:06] Dr. Ellen Price: Anything else?
[10:08] Sofia Varela: Timeline — pilot in Jan sounds good but we need to finalize scope by mid-December.
[10:13] Alex Mercer: We'll aim for a follow-up the week of Dec 8th to lock scope. I'll send the design doc and compliance pack by the end of next week.
[10:20] Dr. Ellen Price: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:23] Alex Mercer: Thanks all — we'll follow up on action items.
